prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Congolese rebels seized a major military camp and a spacious gorilla park in a renewed bout of heavy fighting that sent thousands fleeing, according to the United Nations and park officials. Young gorillas play in Congo's Virunga Park, which was taken over Sunday by rebels fighting army forces. The fighting comes after a tenuous week-old U.N. brokered cease-fire between rebels and government forces fell apart Sunday. Fighting between the rebels under renegade Gen. Laurent Nkunda and Congolese army regulars in the eastern province of North Kivu of the Democratic Republic of the Congo displaced thousands of civilians, according to U.N. spokesman Michele Bonnardeaux. The rebels also seized the headquarters of Virunga National Park in eastern Congo after intense fighting with the Congolese army, according to a statement by park officials. The rebels have used Virunga Park as a base but have never seized its headquarters before. The 3,000 square mile (7,800 square kilometer) park has a gorilla facility and is home to 200 of the 700 endangered mountain gorillas in existence. "Over 50 rangers were forced to flee into the forests and abandon the park station, in fear of their lives," the park statement said. "They have seized the entire gigantic infrastructure [of the park headquarters] which is stategically very close to the main road heading north into Goma," said park spokeswoman Samantha Newport by phone from Goma, about 40 kilometers from the fighting. "The situation is eastern Congo is very dangerous," she said. "It's the first time they've [rebels] ever had the audacity" to take over the park.   Watch as park ranger describes the violence as it explodes behind him » . Newport said the rebels have set up roadblocks so the rangers are making their way through woods south to safety. She said the gorillas and other wildlife in the park are in danger of getting caught in the crossfire. A park ranger described the takeover. "When the rebels started approaching the park station we thought we were all going to be killed," said Park Ranger Bareke Sekibibi, 29, who spoke by cell phone from the forest earlier as he fled, according to the park statement. " We are not military combatants, we are park rangers protecting Virunga's wildlife." Although the civil war in the Congo officially ended in 2003, recent fighting in eastern Congo between government forces and rebels has caused tens of thousands to flee their homes . The conflict and humanitarian crisis in Congo have taken the lives of some 5.4 million people since 1998, and that 45,000 people continue to die there every month, according to an International Rescue Committee report in January.

(CNN) — Congolese rebels seized a major military camp and the expansive Virunga National Park during a renewed bout of heavy fighting that forced thousands of people to flee, according to the United Nations and park officials.

Young gorillas play in Congo’s Virunga Park, which was taken over Sunday by rebels fighting army forces.

The violence erupted after a tenuous, week-old ceasefire brokered by the United Nations between rebels and government forces collapsed Sunday.

Fighting between rebels led by renegade Gen. Laurent Nkunda and regular Congolese army forces in North Kivu, an eastern province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, displaced thousands of civilians, according to U.N. spokesman Michele Bonnardeaux.

The rebels also seized the headquarters of Virunga National Park in eastern Congo following intense fighting with the Congolese army, park officials said in a statement. Although the rebels have previously used Virunga Park as a base, they had never before taken control of its headquarters.

The 3,000-square-mile (7,800-square-kilometer) park includes a gorilla facility and is home to 200 of the world’s 700 remaining endangered mountain gorillas.

“Over 50 rangers were forced to flee into the forests and abandon the park station, in fear of their lives,” the park statement said.

“They have seized the entire gigantic infrastructure [of the park headquarters], which is strategically very close to the main road heading north into Goma,” park spokeswoman Samantha Newport said by phone from Goma, about 40 kilometers from the fighting.

“The situation in eastern Congo is very dangerous,” she said. “It’s the first time they’ve [rebels] ever had the audacity” to take over the park.

Watch as a park ranger describes the violence erupting behind him »

Newport said the rebels had established roadblocks, forcing the rangers to make their way south through the woods to safety. She added that the park’s gorillas and other wildlife were at risk of being caught in the crossfire.

One park ranger described the takeover.

“When the rebels started approaching the park station, we thought we were all going to be killed,” said park ranger Bareke Sekibibi, 29, who spoke by cell phone from the forest while fleeing, according to the park statement. “We are not military combatants; we are park rangers protecting Virunga’s wildlife.”

Although the civil war in Congo officially ended in 2003, recent fighting between government forces and rebels in the country’s east has forced tens of thousands of people to flee their homes.

The conflict and humanitarian crisis in Congo have claimed the lives of approximately 5.4 million people since 1998, while 45,000 people continue to die there each month, according to an International Rescue Committee report published in January.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — The United Nations and park authorities reported that Congolese rebels captured a key military base and a large gorilla reserve during a fresh surge of intense combat that forced thousands of people to escape the area.

The rebels, who are fighting government troops, took control of Congo’s Virunga National Park on Sunday, where young gorillas are among the wildlife protected.

The violence resumed after a fragile ceasefire negotiated by the United Nations one week earlier collapsed on Sunday. According to U.N. spokesperson Michele Bonnardeaux, clashes in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s eastern North Kivu province between fighters loyal to renegade Gen. Laurent Nkunda and regular Congolese army units drove thousands of civilians from their homes.

Park officials said in a statement that the rebels also captured Virunga National Park’s headquarters after fierce fighting with the army. Although rebel forces had previously operated from inside Virunga, they had never before taken over the park’s main offices.

Covering 3,000 square miles, or 7,800 square kilometers, the park includes a gorilla facility and shelters 200 of the world’s 700 remaining endangered mountain gorillas.

“Over 50 rangers were forced to flee into the forests and abandon the park station, in fear of their lives,” the park’s statement said.

Speaking by telephone from Goma, roughly 40 kilometers from the fighting, park spokeswoman Samantha Newport said the rebels had captured the headquarters’ entire extensive complex. She noted that the site is strategically positioned near the principal road running north into Goma.

“The situation in eastern Congo is very dangerous,” Newport said, adding that this was the first time the rebels had been bold enough to occupy the park.

Newport said rebel roadblocks had forced the rangers to travel south through the forest in search of safety. She also warned that the park’s gorillas and other animals could be trapped in the crossfire.

Park ranger Bareke Sekibibi, 29, described the assault while fleeing through the forest and speaking by cellphone, according to the park statement.

“When the rebels started approaching the park station we thought we were all going to be killed,” Sekibibi said. “We are not military combatants, we are park rangers protecting Virunga’s wildlife.”

Although Congo’s civil war officially concluded in 2003, renewed clashes between rebels and government troops in the country’s east have recently forced tens of thousands of residents to leave their homes.

A January report from the International Rescue Committee estimated that conflict and the resulting humanitarian emergency in Congo had killed approximately 5.4 million people since 1998, with another 45,000 continuing to die each month.

More than 50 park rangers escaped into the surrounding forests as rebel forces set up roadblocks around the park headquarters, which occupies a strategically important location. The takeover has raised serious concerns about the safety of Virunga’s wildlife and the people responsible for protecting it.

outputs.L4:
Congolese rebels commanded by Gen. Laurent Nkunda broke a United Nations-brokered cease-fire and seized a major military camp as well as the headquarters of Virunga National Park, U.N. and park officials said. The captures followed heavy fighting between rebel forces and the Congolese army.

Thousands of civilians were forced to flee the area as the clashes intensified. More than 50 park rangers also abandoned Virunga’s headquarters, leaving the protected area and its wildlife increasingly vulnerable.

Virunga is home to exceptional biodiversity, including about 200 of the world’s estimated 700 remaining mountain gorillas. The fighting raised fears for the animals’ safety and made it difficult for conservation workers to patrol the park, monitor wildlife, or prevent poaching and other illegal activity.

The rebel takeover also carried significant military importance. By capturing the camp and surrounding positions, Nkunda’s forces gained control of a strategic site near Goma, the principal city in eastern Congo. The advance threatened to further destabilize the region and underscored the fragility of the cease-fire negotiated by the United Nations.
outputs.L5: CNN reported on the challenges facing Congolese communities amid continued conflict and displacement in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The United Nations has called for greater international support, improved humanitarian access, and renewed diplomatic efforts to protect civilians. Congolese leaders and activists have also urged the global community to address the root causes of instability and help build a more peaceful, united future.

I can’t reproduce CNN’s exact editorial voice, but here’s a concise cable-news-style report:

---

### Congolese rebels seize military camp and Virunga National Park after cease-fire collapses

**KINSHASA, Democratic Republic of Congo** — Rebel forces in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo have seized a key military camp and taken control of parts of Virunga National Park following the collapse of a United Nations-brokered cease-fire, according to local officials and security sources.

The renewed fighting forced Congolese troops to withdraw from the camp as rebels advanced through the surrounding area. Virunga, one of Africa’s oldest national parks and home to endangered mountain gorillas, was also overrun, raising concerns for park employees, nearby communities and wildlife.

The cease-fire had been intended to halt clashes between the Congolese military and the rebel group while mediators pursued negotiations. It was unclear which side fired first after the truce broke down, and independent verification from the conflict zone remained difficult.

Thousands of civilians have fled repeated waves of fighting in eastern Congo, where armed groups have competed for territory and access to valuable mineral resources for decades. Aid agencies have warned that further advances could worsen an already severe humanitarian crisis.

The United Nations called for an immediate end to hostilities and urged all parties to return to negotiations. Congolese authorities said military operations were continuing, while the rebels claimed they had taken the positions after coming under attack.

Virunga National Park has frequently been caught in the region’s violence. Rangers have been killed in previous attacks, and tourism has repeatedly been suspended because of insecurity.
